newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-S.Africa markets rise from the ashes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-S.Africa markets rise from the ashes.

text.p: One year ago rumours about President Nelson Mandela's health and a report from Swiss investment bank UBS that the rand was overvalued sent the currency into a nosedive.
Twelve months on, South Africa is flavour of the month with investors and rand markets are riding high, buoyed by signs that the government is delivering on promised economic reforms.
The currency is at its best level in seven months against a strong dollar, and at a near year-high against the mark and yen. Bond yields are the strongest since the rand meltdown began.

On the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, daily volumes are running at record levels as new money pours in and ING Barings predicts net inflows into the bourse will surge to $2.7 billion this year as funds increase exposure to South Africa.

The laggard of emerging markets in 1996 appears to be back on track, sucking well over three billion rand ($700 million) of foreign money into the local bond market so far this year. Another four billion has gone into offshore rand Eurobond issues.
Rudolph Gouws, economist at Rand Merchant Bank, says the South African story has turned.

The trade balance is improving, foreign exchange reserves are rising and the political picture is clearing, with Deputy President Thabo Mbeki now nearly certain to succeed Mandela as African National Congress leader. The ANC will pick a new leader at the end of the year and whoever is chosen is assumed to be elected country's president in 1999 polls.
"South Africa is in line for quite substantial (budget) deficit reduction, for gradual exchange control abolition and for sticking to conservative monetary policy," he said.
"So while everything is not yet hunky-dory, I think suddenly the markets perceive that maybe the pessimism and cynicism of last year had been overdone."
GETTING TO GRIPS WITH THE DEFICIT

Finance Minister Trevor Manuel announced last week that the government would achieve its targeted budget deficit of 5.1 percent of GDP this year and, more importantly, remain on course to cut it further to four percent in 1997/98.

The rand is still finding a level and markets remain jittery, as underlined when a recent suggestion by Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals that the speed of the rand's advance this year may have been overdone briefly sent it skidding lower.

But economists are nonetheless predicting the currency can outperform inflation differentials in 1997. For the authorities, a lower but stable rand should stimulate both exports, and new inflows of foreign short- and long-term capital.

"We're about 80 cents weaker on the rand than we were last year but the fundamentals are much stronger. We're more confident about the ability to use this country as a platform for exports," Manuel declared.

At the same time, the long-delayed privatisation programme is finally bearing fruit. The sale of a 30 percent stake in telecommunications group Telkom -- sub-Saharan Africa's biggest privatisation yet -- is now imminent.
Final binding bids from four shortlisted foreign firms are due in March with the deal set for completion in April.

Other disposals will follow soon after, including the sale of a substantial chunk of South African Airways to a foreign partner. The first privatisation receipts should start to roll into next year's budget.
AWAITING NEWS ON FOREX CONTROLS
Details of that budget are keenly awaited, not only for evidence of continued fiscal discipline but also for news on further moves to relax exchange controls.
Helped by an improving balance of payments, Manuel is widely expected to announce further steps to lift restrictions in his March 12 budget speech.
Dennis Dykes of Nedcor bank echoes the view of many in the market that an announcement is imminent:

"Certainly I would expect something on exchange controls over the next few weeks, but it will be a part of a gradual process -- they are not going to announce the ending of all exchange controls overnight. Whether that satisfies or dismays the market remains to be seen."
Loosening the reins on currency flows will increase the risk of money fleeing the country, depleting reserves once again.
But given the globalisation of world markets, Reserve Bank's Stals says South Africa has no choice but to let capital out if it wants to attract fresh funds in.

"If you are not prepared to allow South Africans to participate in world financial markets, world financial markets will not be prepared to participate in South Africa," he told journalists in Cape Town last week.
BALANCING CAPITAL FLOWS
Stals -- who has a critical role in advising government on foreign exchange control policy -- stresses it is an evolutionary process that is already well under way.
Some 30 billion rand has already left the country in the last two-and-a-half years and he estimates that 50 percent of the country's exchange controls have already been removed.
But the pent-up demand among South Africans to diversify their assets remains substantial.

Old Mutual, the country's largest life assurance group, signalled recently it could invest up to 25 percent, or 50 billion rand, of its 200 billion in assets overseas once exchange controls were lifted.
The key is balancing those kind of potential outflows with fresh inflows of foreign capital needed to fuel the economy and deliver the target of doubling annual growth to six percent by 2000.

"We have no doubt that South Africa must become part of the international financial markets. South Africa must expose itself to these capital outflows because on balance we are going to get more capital inflows," said Stals.
